newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistanis go to fourth polls in nine years.
newsitem.headline: Pakistanis go to fourth polls in nine years.

text.p: Pakistanis vote on Monday, for fourth time in less than nine years, in national elections that President Farooq Leghari promised would be free, fair and open.

Former prime minister Nawaz Sharif said he was confident of winning. His main rival, Benazir Bhutto, fighting for political survival after Leghari sacked her as prime minister three months ago, accused the president of planning to rig the vote.
"By tomorrow night, we will...complete the process of free, fair and transparent elections," Leghari said in an televised address, hours before the start of voting at 7.00 a.m. (0200 GMT) on Monday.
Polls close at 4.00 p.m. (1100 gmt) with first results late in the evening.
Opinion polls indicated that Sharif would win, but a spokesman for Bhutto dismissed such surveys as media gimmicks arranged by what he called forces seeking to rig the elections.

Bhutto said she had reports that the caretaker government planned to rig the vote in 63 constituencies of the 217-seat National Assembly (lower house) and she would not accept the result if this happened.
Leghari urged people to vote "wisely and selflessly" to elect representatives who could give a good government.

"Pakistan stands at a crossroads," he said. "We need political leaders with vision and courage to steer this country out of the woods. Corruption, waste and inefficiency have eaten into the vitals of our state."

Sharif said he was counting on a comfortable majority in the National Assembly and tackling Pakistan's dire economic problems would be his priority. "The economy is in very bad shape because of the mismanagement of the Benazir Bhutto government," he said.
He told Reuters in his home city of Lahore that repairing the economy would be a long, difficult task, but he was confident that Pakistan could become an "Asian Tiger".

Bhutto, who received a tumultuous welcome from crowds as she drove to her family village of Nuadero in Sindh province, said Pakistan was in "a terrible economic crisis" that only her Pakistan People's Party (PPP) could tackle.
She said neither she nor the nation would accept the result if there was vote-rigging, adding that she had written to Chief Election Commissioner Fakhre Alam about her fears.

Alam said his commission had made arrangements to hold fair elections and he expected a good turnout of voters. Most commentators predicted a low turnout after a lacklustre campaign in the Moslem fasting month of Ramadan.
Corruption has been the main issue in a campaign that failed to excite Pakistanis, many of whom are disillusioned by the perceived misdeeds of the political class.
Leghari sacked Bhutto's government on charges of corruption and misrule, but the caretaker government he appointed has failed to convict any leading politicians or bar them from seeking election.

Bhutto and her husband Asif Ali Zardari, who is held in jail on a charge of conspiring in the murder of his wife's estranged brother Murtaza in September, have denied any wrongdoing, saying they are victims of a plot.

Sharif's previous government was dismissed on corruption charges but was restored by the Supreme Court, only to lose power again two months later. Bhutto's PPP defeated his Pakistan Muslim League party in elections in October 1993.
The Supreme Court last week upheld Leghari's dismissal of Bhutto, saying there was enough evidence of corruption, nepotism and other abuses for him to have fired her.

Former Pakistan cricket captain Imran Khan was the first to focus public attention on the corruption issue, but polls suggest his Tehrik-i-Insaaf Pakistan (PTI) party is unlikely to win more than a few seats.
